claims.claim: YAP1-TFE3 fuses exon one from YAP1 in frame to exon 4 of TFE3.
claims.source: Similarly, YAP1-TFE3 fuses exon one from YAP1 in frame to exon 4 of TFE3 resulting in the N terminus of YAP fused in frame to the C terminus of TFE3.
claims.evidence: This claim describes the molecular structure of the YAP-TFE3 fusion, supported by previous characterization studies.

claims.claim: The N terminus of YAP contains the TEAD-binding domain.
claims.source: The N terminus of YAP contains the TEAD-binding domain (Gaffney et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A showing the domain structure and citation to a study that characterized YAP domains.

claims.claim: The C terminus of TFE3 contains the transactivating domain, basic helix loop helix domain, and leucine zipper.
claims.source: The C terminus of TFE3 contains the transactivating domain, basic helix loop helix domain, and leucine zipper (Antonescu et al., 2013; Kauffman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the functional domains of TFE3.

claims.claim: TFE3 is a member of the MiTF family of basic helix-loop-helix containing transcription factors.
claims.source: TFE3 is a member of the MiTF family of basic helix-loop-helix containing transcription factors, consisting of four structurally similar genes (TFE3, TFE3B, TFEC, and MITF), that are involved in regulating tissue-specific functions of cell differentiation (Kauffman et al., 2014; Steingrimsson et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the MiTF family of transcription factors.

claims.claim: TFE3 activates transcription by binding to the µE3 motif within the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer.
claims.source: TFE3 is ubiquitously expressed and activates transcription by binding to the µE3 motif within the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer (Beckmann et al., 1990; Henthorn et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the DNA-binding specificity of TFE3.

claims.claim: TFE3 promotes cell survival in starvation conditions by regulating lysosomal biogenesis and homeostasis.
claims.source: TFE3 has recently been shown to promote cell survival in starvation conditions by regulating lysosomal biogenesis and homeostasis while also having a role in clearance of cellular debris (Martina et al., 2014; Slade and Pulinilkunnil, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the cellular functions of TFE3.

claims.claim: TFE3 is involved in gene fusions in renal cell carcinoma and alveolar soft part sarcoma.
claims.source: TFE3 is also involved in gene fusions in renal cell carcinoma and alveolar soft part sarcoma (Kauffman et al., 2014; Argani et al., 2003; Klatte et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that identified TFE3 fusions in other cancer types.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 promotes anchorage independent growth while full length YAP, full-length TFE3, or the truncated portions of YAP or TFE3 present in the fusion protein do not.
claims.source: YAP-TFE3 promoted anchorage independent growth while full length YAP, full-length TFE3, or the truncated portions of YAP or TFE3 present in the fusion protein did not.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar assay data (Figure 1B) and poly-HEMA assay data (Figure 1C, D) showing that only the fusion protein promotes anchorage-independent growth.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 is a neomorphic protein combining properties of both YAP and TFE3 to transform cells.
claims.source: The above findings indicate that YAP-TFE3 is a neomorphic protein combining properties of both YAP and TFE3 to transform cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that neither full-length protein nor truncated portions alone can recapitulate the transforming activity of the fusion.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 remained predominantly nuclear under confluent conditions while YAP was enriched in the cytoplasm and its abundance was reduced.
claims.source: Under confluent conditions, YAP was enriched in the cytoplasm and its abundance was reduced, while YAP-TFE3 remained predominantly nuclear (Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 1E-F) showing differential localization of YAP and YAP-TFE3 under confluent conditions.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 remained in the nucleus upon cell confluence while YAP was no longer localized in the nucleus and instead accumulated in the cytoplasm where it was subsequently degraded.
claims.source: Nuclear and cytoplasmic fractionation confirmed that YAP was no longer localized in the nucleus and instead accumulated in the cytoplasm where it was subsequently degraded. In contrast, YAP-TFE3 remained in the nucleus upon cell confluence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) showing differential localization and stability of YAP versus YAP-TFE3.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 remained constitutively nuclear upon cell detachment while YAP localization shifted from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
claims.source: Similarly, YAP localization shifted from the nucleus to the cytoplasm upon cell detachment, while YAP-TFE3 remained constitutively nuclear (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation data during a time course of cell detachment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 is no longer subject to Hippo pathway-mediated suppression because the key residues targeted by LATS1/2 (S127 and S381) are not present in YAP-TFE3.
claims.source: Taken together, the above data suggest that YAP-TFE3 is no longer subject to Hippo pathway-mediated suppression, likely because the key residues targeted by LATS1/2 (S127 and S381) (Zhao et al., 2007) are not present in YAP-TFE3.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that YAP-TFE3 remains nuclear under conditions that normally trigger Hippo pathway activation, combined with knowledge that key LATS phosphorylation sites are absent.

claims.claim: Mice with NIH 3T3-derived tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 demonstrated a shorter overall survival compared to empty vector.
claims.source: Mice with NIH 3T3-derived tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 demonstrated a shorter overall survival compared to empty vector (p<0.0001 for both YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1) (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data (Figure 1G) showing reduced survival in mice with fusion protein-expressing tumors.

claims.claim: Time to tumor initiation was similar for NIH 3T3 cells expressing either YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 fusion protein.
claims.source: Tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 formed palpable masses ~ 7 days post-injection (Figure 1H) indicating time to tumor initiation was similar for NIH 3T3 cells expressing either fusion protein.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data (Figure 1H) showing similar kinetics of tumor formation for both fusion proteins.

claims.claim: NIH 3T3 cells containing empty vector formed tumors, but tumor initiation was delayed by approximately 10 days compared to fusion protein-expressing cells.
claims.source: NIH 3T3 cells containing empty vector formed tumors, as has been described (Greig et al., 1985), but tumor initiation was delayed by approximately 10 days.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data (Figure 1H) and citation to a previous study showing that NIH 3T3 cells can form tumors.

claims.claim: The slopes of the growth curves for YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 were similar to empty vector, confirmed by Ki-67 labeling.
claims.source: The slopes of the growth curves for the two fusion proteins were similar to empty vector, and this was confirmed by Ki-67 labeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data (Figure 1H) and Ki-67 immunohistochemistry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).

claims.claim: NIH 3T3 cell-derived tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 exhibited a more rounded (epithelioid) cytomorphology and a greater degree of cellular pleomorphism compared to control tumors.
claims.source: NIH 3T3 cell-derived tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 exhibited a more rounded (epithelioid) cytomorphology and a greater degree of cellular pleomorphism as compared to control tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis (H&E staining) shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Microscopic metastases were present in the lungs of mice with YAP-TFE3-expressing tumors but not TAZ-CAMTA1-expressing tumors.
claims.source: Necropsy and pathological evaluation of the lungs demonstrated the presence of microscopic metastases in the YAP-TFE3 (p=0.0299) but not the TAZ-CAMTA1 (not significant) cohorts (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of lung tissue and quantification of metastases (Figure 1I).

claims.claim: Expression of YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 decreased latency to tumor formation compared to empty vector in SW872 cells in vivo.
claims.source: In the mildly tumorigenic SW872 cell line (Stratford et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013a; Li et al., 2014), expression of YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 decreased latency to tumor formation compared to empty vector in vivo (Figure 1J), similar to NIH 3T3 cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data for SW872 xenografts (Figure 1J).

claims.claim: The S51A mutant of TAZ-CAMTA1 significantly reduced colony formation in soft agar and growth on poly-HEMA while the TAZ-CAMTA1ΔWW mutant did not.
claims.source: While the S51A mutant (disrupts TEAD binding) of TAZ-CAMTA1 significantly reduced colony formation in soft agar/growth on poly-HEMA (Tanas et al., 2016), the TAZ-CAMTA1ΔWW mutant did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar and poly-HEMA assay data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G) comparing different TAZ-CAMTA1 mutants.

claims.claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 function is dependent on the TEAD binding domain but not the WW domain.
claims.source: This confirms that TAZ-CAMTA1 function is dependent on the TEAD binding domain but not the WW domain.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differential effects of mutations in the TEAD binding domain versus the WW domain on TAZ-CAMTA1 function.

claims.claim: Knock-down of Tead1 reduced anchorage independent growth on poly-HEMA and in soft agar in NIH-3T3 cells expressing YAP-TFE3.
claims.source: Knock-down of Tead1 reduced anchorage independent growth on poly-HEMA (Figure 2B) and in soft agar (Figure 2C) with two different short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by poly-HEMA assay data (Figure 2B) and soft agar assay data (Figure 2C) after Tead1 knockdown.

claims.claim: The YAP-TFE3 S94A mutation completely abrogated YAP-TFE3-driven anchorage-independent growth on poly-HEMA and in soft agar.
claims.source: The S94A mutation completely abrogated YAP-TFE3-driven anchorage-independent growth on poly-HEMA (Figure 2E) and in soft agar (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by poly-HEMA assay data (Figure 2E) and soft agar assay data (Figure 2F) comparing YAP-TFE3 to the S94A mutant.

claims.claim: The YAP-TFE3 S94A mutant showed a sevenfold decrease in expression of Ccn2(Ctgf) compared to the YAP-TFE3 control.
claims.source: By quantitative RT-PCR, the YAP-TFE3 S94A mutant showed a sevenfold decrease in expression of Ccn2(Ctgf), a YAP target gene, compared to the YAP-TFE3 control (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data (Figure 2G) comparing gene expression between YAP-TFE3 and the S94A mutant.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 S94A showed a sixfold decrease in CCN2 promoter binding compared to YAP-TFE3 control by ChIP-qPCR.
claims.source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation-quantitative PCR for the CCN2 promoter (which contains the TEAD-binding sequence) showed a sixfold decrease in CCN2 promoter binding by YAP-TFE3 S94A as compared to YAP-TFE3 control (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 2H) showing reduced binding of the S94A mutant to the CCN2 promoter.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 S94A showed decreased luciferase activity compared to the YAP-TFE3 control using the 8XGTIIC luciferase reporter.
claims.source: Using the 8XGTIIC luciferase reporter containing eight TEAD consensus binding sequences (Dupont et al., 2011), YAP-TFE3 S94A showed decreased luciferase activity compared to the YAP-TFE3 control (Figure 2I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data (Figure 2I) comparing YAP-TFE3 to the S94A mutant.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3, like TAZ-CAMTA1, requires TEAD transcription factors to drive its oncogenic transcriptional program.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that YAP-TFE3, like TAZ-CAMTA1, requires TEAD transcription factors to drive its oncogenic transcriptional program (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence showing that disrupting TEAD binding abolishes YAP-TFE3 function.

claims.claim: 70% of genes differentially expressed in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome were also present in the TAZ4SA transcriptome.
claims.source: Differentially expressed genes (FDR < 0.05) showed considerable overlap between the TAZ4SA and TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptomes; 70% of genes differentially expressed in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome were also present in the TAZ4SA transcriptome with a –log10[hypergeometric density] (HGD) of 105.6 (p=1.92×10−106).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis comparing the TAZ-CAMTA1 and TAZ4SA transcriptomes.

claims.claim: 9% of genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome overlapped with the CAMTA1 gene set.
claims.source: By comparison, a much smaller percentage of overlap (9%) was identified between the TAZ-CAMTA1 and CAMTA1 gene sets with an HGD of 34.1 (p=4.71×10−35).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis comparing the TAZ-CAMTA1 and CAMTA1 transcriptomes.

claims.claim: 29% of differentially expressed genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptional program in NIH 3T3 cells were not induced by either TAZ4SA or CAMTA1.
claims.source: A significant percentage (29%) of differentially expressed genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptional program were not induced by either TAZ4SA or CAMTA1 (Figure 3A; Figure 3—source data 1) in NIH 3T3 cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3A) showing unique genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome.

claims.claim: 31% of the TAZ-CAMTA1 gene set in SW872 cells were unique and not found in the TAZ or CAMTA1 transcriptional programs.
claims.source: Similarly, 31% of the TAZ-CAMTA1 gene set in SW872 cells were unique and not found in the TAZ or CAMTA1 transcriptional programs (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3B) showing unique genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome in SW872 cells.

claims.claim: 78% of genes differentially expressed in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome in NIH 3T3 cells were present in the YAP5SA transcriptional program.
claims.source: In NIH 3T3 cells, 78% of genes differentially expressed in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome were present in the YAP5SA transcriptional program.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis comparing the YAP-TFE3 and YAP5SA transcriptomes.

claims.claim: 10% of differentially expressed genes in the YAP-TFE3 gene set in NIH 3T3 cells were also present in the TFE3 transcriptome.
claims.source: Comparatively, only 10% of differentially expressed genes in the YAP-TFE3 gene set were also present in the TFE3 transcriptome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis comparing the YAP-TFE3 and TFE3 transcriptomes.

claims.claim: 20% of the differentially expressed genes in NIH 3T3 cells were unique to the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome and not found in the YAP5SA or TFE3 transcriptional programs.
claims.source: In NIH 3T3 cells 20% of the differentially expressed genes were unique to the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome and not found in the YAP5SA or TFE3 transcriptional programs (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3C) showing unique genes in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome.

claims.claim: 47% of the YAP-TFE3 transcriptional program in SW872 cells was found only in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome and not in YAP5SA or TFE3 controls.
claims.source: Similarly, in SW872 cells 47% of the YAP-TFE3 transcriptional program was found only in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome and not in YAP5SA or TFE3 controls (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3D) showing unique genes in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome in SW872 cells.

claims.claim: The TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 transcriptomes in NIH 3T3 cells grouped more closely together than the transcriptomes of their cognate full length proteins.
claims.source: A principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 transcriptomes in NIH 3T3 cells grouped more closely together than the transcriptomes of their cognate full length proteins (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3E) showing clustering of samples.

claims.claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 promote upregulation of the well-defined TAZ/YAP transcriptional targets CCN2(CTGF)/Ccn2 and CCN1(CYR61)/Ccn1.
claims.source: This was corroborated by qRT-PCR experiments, which showed that TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 promote upregulation of the well-defined TAZ/YAP transcriptional targets CCN2(CTGF)/Ccn2 and CCN1(CYR61)/Ccn1, but also genes unique to the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 transcriptomes such as Fras1 (an extracellular matrix protein), Erbb3 (Erb-B2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinase 3) (Figure 3F), and FBLN5 (an extracellular matrix protein) (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR validation data (Figure 3F and 3G) confirming RNA-Seq findings.

claims.claim: The top cancer-related signatures activated by TAZ-CAMTA1 in SW872 cells are the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, Hippo signaling pathway, focal adhesion, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interaction.
claims.source: iPathwayGuide analysis performed showed that the top cancer-related signatures activated by TAZ-CAMTA1 in SW872 cells (Figure 3H) are the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, Hippo signaling pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), focal adhesion, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interaction (mirroring qRT-PCR results in Figure 3F and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by iPathwayGuide analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3H) showing enriched pathways.

claims.claim: The top cancer-related signatures activated by YAP-TFE3 in SW872 cells included the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, MAPK signaling pathway, and JAK-STAT signaling pathway.
claims.source: The top cancer-related signatures activated by YAP-TFE3 in SW872 cells (Figure 3I) also included the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, as well as the MAPK and JAK-STAT signaling pathways.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by iPathwayGuide analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3I) showing enriched pathways.

claims.claim: CAMTA1 and TFE3 ChIP peaks were localized in closer proximity to the TSS (0-1 kb) compared to TAZ4SA, TAZ-CAMTA1, YAP5SA, and YAP-TFE3.
claims.source: Annotation of ChIP peaks with respect to their nearest gene transcriptional start site (TSS) demonstrated that CAMTA1 and TFE3 ChIP peaks were localized in closer proximity to the TSS (0–1 kb). In contrast, TAZ4SA, TAZ-CAMTA1, YAP5SA, and YAP-TFE3 predominantly occupied distal intergenic sequences (3 kb or greater) consistent with active enhancer sequences (Figure 4A–E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis showing the distribution of binding sites relative to the TSS (Figure 4A-E).

claims.claim: 69% of TAZ-CAMTA1 distal intergenic sequences overlap with H3K27ac ChIP peaks.
claims.source: as confirmed by the presence of overlapping H3K27ac ChIP peaks (Zhang et al., 2013b; Creyghton et al., 2010; Calo and Wysocka, 2013) (69% overlap in TAZ-CAMTA1 distal intergenic sequences; 68% overlap in YAP-TFE3 distal intergenic sequences) (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of overlapping ChIP-Seq peaks for TAZ-CAMTA1 and H3K27ac (Figure 4D).

claims.claim: 68% of YAP-TFE3 distal intergenic sequences overlap with H3K27ac ChIP peaks.
claims.source: as confirmed by the presence of overlapping H3K27ac ChIP peaks (Zhang et al., 2013b; Creyghton et al., 2010; Calo and Wysocka, 2013) (69% overlap in TAZ-CAMTA1 distal intergenic sequences; 68% overlap in YAP-TFE3 distal intergenic sequences) (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of overlapping ChIP-Seq peaks for YAP-TFE3 and H3K27ac (Figure 4E).

claims.claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 maintain the genomic occupancy characteristics of increased preference for distal intergenic/enhancer sequences as demonstrated by TAZ and YAP, but also occupy sequences proximal to the TSS.
claims.source: Thus TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 maintain the genomic occupancy characteristics of increased preference for distal intergenic/enhancer sequences as demonstrated by TAZ and YAP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C; Zanconato et al., 2015; Galli et al., 2015; Stein et al., 2015), but also occupy sequences proximal to the TSS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis (Figure 4C-E) and citations to previous studies characterizing TAZ/YAP genomic occupancy.

claims.claim: 56% of TAZ-CAMTA1 genes containing ChIP peaks were present in the TAZ-CAMTA1 data set, but not the TAZ4SA or CAMTA1 data sets.
claims.source: Mirroring the RNA-Seq data, 56% of TAZ-CAMTA1 genes containing ChIP peaks were present in the TAZ-CAMTA1 data set, but not the TAZ4SA or CAMTA1 data sets (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4F) showing unique genes bound by TAZ-CAMTA1.

claims.claim: 46% of YAP-TFE3 genes containing ChIP peaks were unique to the YAP-TFE3 data set and not present in the YAP5SA or TFE3 controls.
claims.source: Similarly, 46% of YAP-TFE3 genes containing ChIP peaks were unique to the YAP-TFE3 data set and not present in the YAP5SA or TFE3 controls (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4G) showing unique genes bound by YAP-TFE3.

claims.claim: The chromatin binding profile of TAZ-CAMTA1 more closely resembled TAZ4SA than CAMTA1.
claims.source: Overall, the chromatin binding profile of TAZ-CAMTA1 more closely resembled TAZ4SA (HGD of 52.9) than CAMTA1 (HGD of 43.8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric analysis of ChIP-Seq data comparing the overlap between different datasets.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 bound chromatin was more like that of YAP5SA than TFE3.
claims.source: Likewise, YAP-TFE3 bound chromatin was more like that of YAP5SA (HGD of 166.8) than TFE3 (HGD of 11.8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric analysis of ChIP-Seq data comparing the overlap between different datasets.

claims.claim: Approximately the same proportion of TAZ4SA and TAZ-CAMTA1 peaks contained the TEAD binding sequence (58% vs. 61%, respectively).
claims.source: Unbiased motif enrichment analysis (Figure 4—source data 1) showed that approximately the same proportion of TAZ4SA and TAZ-CAMTA1 peaks contained the TEAD binding sequence (58% vs. 61%, respectively) (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4F).

claims.claim: There was a decrease in the frequency of FOS/JUN binding sites in TAZ-CAMTA1 (31%) as compared to TAZ4SA (50%).
claims.source: Interestingly, there was a decrease in the frequency of FOS/JUN binding sites in TAZ-CAMTA1 (31%) as compared to TAZ4SA (50%), which appeared to be offset by an increase in Early growth response gene-2 (EGR2) binding motifs (23% vs. 13% for TAZ4SA).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claims.claim: There was an increase in EGR2 binding motifs in TAZ-CAMTA1 (23%) compared to TAZ4SA (13%).
claims.source: Interestingly, there was a decrease in the frequency of FOS/JUN binding sites in TAZ-CAMTA1 (31%) as compared to TAZ4SA (50%), which appeared to be offset by an increase in Early growth response gene-2 (EGR2) binding motifs (23% vs. 13% for TAZ4SA).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claims.claim: The fraction of YAP-TFE3-bound peaks containing the TEAD-binding sequence (38%) was decreased compared to YAP5SA-bound peaks (51%).
claims.source: Motif enrichment analysis showed a decrease in the fraction of YAP-TFE3-bound peaks containing the TEAD-binding sequence (38%) as compared to YAP5SA-bound peaks (51%) (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4G).

claims.claim: The MiTF binding motif was enriched in YAP-TFE3 (58%) compared to YAP5SA (16%).
claims.source: Interestingly, the MiTF binding motif was enriched in YAP-TFE3 (58%) compared to YAP5SA (16%) (Figure 4G), suggesting that, like TAZ-CAMTA1, TFE3 confers DNA binding properties to the YAP-TFE3 protein in addition to events mediated by YAP's interaction with TEAD transcription factors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4G).

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 co-immunoprecipitates with TFE3.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we found that YAP-TFE3 indeed co-immunoprecipitates with TFE3, and that disruption of the bHLH domain in the TFE3 portion of YAP-TFE3 that is responsible for dimerization altered anchorage-independent growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) showing interaction between YAP-TFE3 and TFE3.

claims.claim: Disruption of the bHLH domain in the TFE3 portion of YAP-TFE3 altered anchorage-independent growth.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we found that YAP-TFE3 indeed co-immunoprecipitates with TFE3, and that disruption of the bHLH domain in the TFE3 portion of YAP-TFE3 that is responsible for dimerization altered anchorage-independent growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar assay data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) showing reduced colony formation with the bHLH domain mutant.

claims.claim: 13% of differentially expressed genes for TAZ-CAMTA1 were directly bound by the transcription factor.
claims.source: Thirteen percent of differentially expressed genes for TAZ-CAMTA1 were directly bound by the transcription factor (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).

claims.claim: 15% of differentially expressed genes for YAP-TFE3 were directly bound by the fusion protein.
claims.source: Similarly, 15% of differentially expressed genes for YAP-TFE3 were directly bound by the fusion protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).

claims.claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 and CAMTA1 preferentially opened chromatin in areas of the genome more distal to the TSS than TAZ4SA.
claims.source: Heat map and histogram analysis of ATAC peaks showed that TAZ-CAMTA1 and CAMTA1 preferentially opened chromatin in areas of the genome more distal to the TSS than TAZ4SA (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-Seq data analysis (Figure 5A) showing the distribution of accessible chromatin relative to the TSS.

claims.claim: YAP-TFE3 preferentially opened chromatin architecture more distal to the TSS than YAP5SA.
claims.source: Similarly, although less pronounced, YAP-TFE3 preferentially opened chromatin architecture more distal to the TSS than YAP5SA (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-Seq data analysis (Figure 5B) showing the distribution of accessible chromatin relative to the TSS.

claims.claim: The accessible chromatin profile of TAZ-CAMTA1 most closely resembled that of CAMTA1.
claims.source: However, hypergeometric analysis showed that the accessible chromatin profile of TAZ-CAMTA1 most closely resembled that of CAMTA1 (Figure 5C)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric analysis of ATAC-Seq data (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: The hypergeometric density between YAP-TFE3 and YAP5SA (106.0) was roughly equivalent to that between YAP-TFE3 and TFE3 (98.0).
claims.source: while the -log10(hypergeometric density) HGD between YAP-TFE3 and YAP5SA (106.0) was roughly equivalent to that between YAP-TFE3 and TFE3 (98.0) (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric analysis of ATAC-Seq data (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: Both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 promoted chromatin accessibility for unique genes not found in the control data sets.
claims.source: This analysis (Figure 5C,D) also showed that both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 promoted chromatin accessibility for unique genes not found in the control data sets, making them available for either transcriptional activation or repression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of ATAC-Seq data (Figure 5C, D) showing unique accessible chromatin regions.

claims.claim: More transposase accessible, non-baseline genes were present with expression of TAZ-CAMTA1 (3147 genes) and YAP-TFE3 (2499 genes) than TAZ4SA (656 genes) and YAP5SA (1629 genes), respectively.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis (Figure 8A) and is an inference based on the observation that YAP-TFE3 interacts with fewer epigenetic modifiers.

claims.claim: The most down-regulated genes after YEATS2 or ZZZ3 knockdown in TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 expressing cells showed an enrichment of extracellular matrix proteins (FBLN5, SPP1, GPC4, and LAMA1).
claims.source: Aligning the most down-regulated genes for TAZ-CAMTA1 shYEATS2, TAZ-CAMTA1 shZZZ3, YAP-TFE3 shYEATS2, and YAP-TFE3 shZZZ3 revealed an enrichment of extracellular matrix proteins (FBLN5, SPP1, GPC4, and LAMA1) (Figure 8B and Figure 8—source data 1) and validated by qRT-PCR (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis (Figure 8B) and qRT-PCR validation (Figure 8C) after YEATS2 or ZZZ3 knockdown.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by iPathwayGuide analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 8D) after YEATS2 or ZZZ3 knockdown.

claims.source: We found that 71% of differentially expressed genes (DEG) with YEATS2 knock-down and 74% of DEG with ZZZ3 knock-down were within euchromatin unique to YAP-TFE3 expressing cells (Figure 8E,F).

claims.source: We found that 71% of differentially expressed genes (DEG) with YEATS2 knock-down and 74% of DEG with ZZZ3 knock-down were within euchromatin unique to YAP-TFE3 expressing cells (Figure 8E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ATAC-Seq data (Figure 8F) after ZZZ3 knockdown.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (Figure 8J) using TCGA sarcoma data.

claims.claim: The ATAC complex may be a key oncogenic driver in multiple sarcomas in addition to EHE.
claims.source: Via Kaplan-Meier analysis, we showed that increased expression of YEATS2 (Figure 8I) or ZZZ3 (Figure 8J) predicted a poorer prognosis across different histological types of sarcoma, suggesting the ATAC complex may be a key oncogenic driver in multiple sarcomas in addition to EHE.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that YEATS2 and ZZZ3 expression predicts poor prognosis across multiple sarcoma types.

claims.claim: The ATAC complex is a key epigenetic mediator of the oncogenic properties of both the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 fusion proteins.
claims.source: Here, we provide new insights into the endothelial cancer EHE by studying the disease defining fusion proteins TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3. We find that each fusion protein drives a related but distinct transcriptional program, which is underpinned by the fact that they both engage the genome at least in part via the TEAD transcription factors, as do wild-type YAP and TAZ. Mechanistically, using a paired proteomic and genomic screen, we identify the ATAC complex as a key epigenetic mediator enabling both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 to modulate the chromatin environment and transcription, thus transforming cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is a summary statement supported by the combined results of BioID, RNAi screen, and functional assays presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The ATAC complex represents a potential therapeutic target for EHE, regardless of which fusion protein it harbors.
claims.source: Importantly, our study also indicates that the ATAC complex represents a potential therapeutic target for EHE, a sarcoma currently lacking an effective medical therapy, regardless of which fusion protein it harbors.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that the ATAC complex is required for the oncogenic function of both fusion proteins.

results.result: EHE is a vascular sarcoma characterized by two mutually exclusive gene fusions: WWTR1-CAMTA1 (85-90% of cases) and YAP1-TFE3 (10-15% of cases), and lacks effective medical therapy.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6, and C7 establish the clinical and molecular characteristics of EHE based on established knowledge and prior literature. These are well-documented facts about the disease supported by multiple citations.

results.result: YAP-TFE3 is a neomorphic fusion protein that transforms cells through combined properties of YAP and TFE3, remains constitutively nuclear under conditions that normally trigger Hippo pathway suppression, and escapes Hippo pathway regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 are supported by multiple complementary assays including soft agar, poly-HEMA, immunofluorescence, and nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation (Figures 1B-F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The data consistently show that YAP-TFE3 remains nuclear under confluence and detachment conditions where wild-type YAP is cytoplasmic and degraded.

results.result: Both YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 fusion proteins drive tumor formation in vivo with reduced latency compared to controls, and YAP-TFE3 promotes metastasis to the lungs.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are supported by xenograft experiments in NSG mice using both NIH 3T3 and SW872 cells (Figures 1G-J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The data show statistically significant differences in survival, tumor initiation, and metastasis. However, the experiments were repeated only twice with 5-10 mice per group, which is modest but acceptable for xenograft studies.

results.result: Both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 require TEAD transcription factors to drive their oncogenic transcriptional programs, as demonstrated by loss of function with TEAD binding domain mutations and TEAD knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 are supported by multiple complementary approaches including mutagenesis studies, shRNA knockdown, soft agar assays, poly-HEMA assays, qRT-PCR, ChIP-qPCR, and luciferase reporter assays (Figures 1—figure supplement 2F-G, Figures 2A-I). The convergent evidence from different experimental modalities strongly supports the requirement for TEAD binding.

results.result: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 drive transcriptomes that significantly overlap with TAZ/YAP but also contain substantial unique gene sets (20-47% depending on cell line), indicating the fusion proteins create distinct transcriptional programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C58 are supported by RNA-Seq data in biological triplicates across two cell lines (NIH 3T3 and SW872) with appropriate statistical analysis (FDR < 0.05) and validation by qRT-PCR (Figures 3A-G). The hypergeometric analysis provides quantitative support for the overlap and uniqueness of the transcriptomes. PCA analysis confirms the distinct clustering patterns.

results.result: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 activate cancer-related signaling pathways including PI3K-Akt, Hippo, MAPK, and JAK-STAT pathways, as well as pathways related to focal adhesion and extracellular matrix.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by iPathwayGuide analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figures 3H-I) and validated by qRT-PCR for specific genes (Figures 3F-G). The pathway analysis is appropriate for the data type and the validation strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 bind predominantly to distal intergenic/enhancer sequences marked by H3K27ac, maintain TEAD binding motif enrichment, but also show enrichment for non-TEAD motifs (EGR2 for TAZ-CAMTA1, MiTF for YAP-TFE3), indicating altered DNA binding properties compared to wild-type TAZ/YAP.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C73 are supported by ChIP-Seq data in biological triplicates with appropriate controls and validation by ChIP-qPCR (Figures 4A-H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The motif enrichment analysis is unbiased and the overlap with H3K27ac marks provides independent validation of enhancer binding. The hypergeometric analysis quantifies the similarities and differences between fusion proteins and controls.

results.result: YAP-TFE3 co-immunoprecipitates with full-length TFE3, and disruption of the bHLH dimerization domain reduces anchorage-independent growth, suggesting TFE3 dimerization contributes to YAP-TFE3 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation and soft agar assay data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A). However, the mechanistic interpretation could be strengthened with additional experiments examining whether the bHLH mutation specifically disrupts TFE3 dimerization or has other effects on protein stability or localization.

results.result: Only 13-15% of differentially expressed genes are directly bound by the fusion proteins, indicating that the majority of transcriptional changes are indirect.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-B). This is an important observation that suggests the fusion proteins work through both direct and indirect mechanisms. The low percentage of direct targets is consistent with transcription factor biology where secondary effects are common.

results.result: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 increase chromatin accessibility, particularly at distal regions from the TSS, with TAZ-CAMTA1 chromatin profile resembling CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 showing intermediate similarity to both YAP5SA and TFE3, and the majority of bound and differentially expressed genes are within euchromatin regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C85 are supported by ATAC-Seq data in biological triplicates with appropriate analysis including hypergeometric testing and PCA (Figures 5A-G). The integration of ATAC-Seq with RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data provides strong evidence for the chromatin remodeling function of the fusion proteins. The quantitative analysis showing more accessible genes with fusion proteins than controls is compelling.

results.result: BioID mass spectrometry identified 27 shared proximity interactors between TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3, enriched for epigenetic/transcriptional regulators including histone modifying enzymes, transcriptional regulators, and chromatin remodeling proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are supported by BioID mass spectrometry in biological duplicates with SAINT analysis (Figures 6A-E). The filtering strategy to identify shared interactors is reasonable, though the requirement for increased interaction relative to full-length TAZ/YAP may exclude some relevant interactors. The functional classification is appropriate and informative.

results.result: YEATS2 and ZZZ3, the top hits from the RNAi screen, are components of the ATAC histone acetyltransferase complex, and KAT14, a third ATAC complex subunit, was also identified by BioID, establishing the ATAC complex as a key interactor.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by the RNAi screen results (Figure 7C) and BioID data (Figure 6C). The convergence of two independent approaches (functional screen and proximity labeling) strongly supports the importance of the ATAC complex. The background information about ATAC complex function is well-cited.

results.result: Knockdown of YEATS2 or ZZZ3 reduces anchorage-independent growth in TAZ-CAMTA1-expressing cells, and KAT14 shows the strongest interaction with both fusion proteins by co-immunoprecipitation among ATAC complex subunits.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by soft agar assays after shRNA knockdown (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-D) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E-G). The validation of BioID results by co-IP strengthens the conclusions. However, the experiments were repeated only twice, which is modest.

results.result: Knockdown of YEATS2 or ZZZ3 alters the fusion protein transcriptomes, with greater effect on YAP-TFE3 than TAZ-CAMTA1, downregulating extracellular matrix proteins and key signaling pathways including MAPK and PI3K-Akt.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are supported by RNA-Seq after ATAC complex knockdown in biological duplicates with validation by qRT-PCR (Figures 8A-D, Figure 8—figure supplement 2). The PCA analysis shows clear separation of knockdown samples from controls. The pathway analysis is appropriate and the validation by qRT-PCR strengthens the conclusions. However, biological duplicates are less robust than triplicates.

results.result: 71-74% of differentially expressed genes after YEATS2 or ZZZ3 knockdown are within euchromatin regions unique to YAP-TFE3-expressing cells, linking ATAC complex function to chromatin accessibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ATAC-Seq data (Figures 8E-F). This analysis provides mechanistic insight linking the ATAC complex to the chromatin remodeling function of the fusion proteins. The high percentage of affected genes within fusion-specific euchromatin is compelling evidence.

results.result: Vitronectin is expressed in all EHE clinical samples but essentially absent in epithelioid angiosarcoma and epithelioid hemangioma, suggesting it may be a diagnostic marker.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by immunohistochemistry on clinical samples (Figure 8H). The sample size (6 EHE, 6 epithelioid hemangioma, 5 epithelioid angiosarcoma) is modest but reasonable for a pilot study. The specificity of vitronectin expression for EHE is notable, though larger validation studies would strengthen this finding.

results.result: Increased expression of YEATS2 or ZZZ3 predicts poorer prognosis across different sarcoma types in TCGA data, suggesting the ATAC complex may be a key oncogenic driver in multiple sarcomas beyond EHE.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis using TCGA sarcoma data (Figures 8I-J). The analysis shows statistically significant associations between ATAC complex expression and survival. However, this is a correlative analysis across heterogeneous sarcoma types, and the mechanistic inference (C108) requires additional validation in other sarcoma models.

results.result: The ATAC complex is a key epigenetic mediator of both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 oncogenic function, enabling the fusion proteins to simultaneously hyperactivate TEAD-based transcription and modulate chromatin environment, representing a potential therapeutic target for EHE.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5, C109-C110 represent the central conclusion of the manuscript, supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: BioID identifying ATAC complex interaction, RNAi screen showing functional requirement, RNA-Seq showing transcriptional dependence, ATAC-Seq showing chromatin effects, and co-IP validating interactions. The therapeutic potential (C110) is a reasonable inference but remains speculative without actual therapeutic studies.
